title: Elastic Representations via Hyperbolic Geometry
claim: A lightweight post-hoc adaptor on a frozen encoder yields elastic embeddings at far lower training cost than retraining baselines.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right pipeline plus scatter plot, shaded optimal-zone box
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a), on the left and taking most of the width, is a left-to-right pipeline. An image icon and a text icon feed a frozen encoder, drawn as a snowflake-marked trapezoid. The encoder outputs a vector z in R^d. This goes into a dashed yellow Projector box that holds two MLP blocks with flame icons, meaning they are trainable. The outputs are stacked embeddings z1 (low-dimensional, purple) and z2 (higher-dimensional, gold). An expmap arrow links them to a 3D Lorentzian hyperboloid surface. A label reads 'Hyperbolic Contrastive Loss'. Panel (b), on the right, is a scatter plot of average 1-NN accuracy against GPU hours. HERL (Ours) is a red dot in a green shaded 'Optimal operating zone' at top-left. MRL, MRL-E, SVD and Rand. FS are placed elsewhere in the plot. The eye goes first to the colorful pipeline.
caption: Overview. (a) We propose Hyperbolic Elastic Representation Learning (HERL), a post-hoc adaptor (without encoder retraining) that utilizes the inherent exponential volume capacity and faithful structural preservation properties of hyperbolic geometry. (b) HERL enables elastic representations at a fraction of the training cost. Approximately two hours to train representations of size 8 to 8192, on a single H100 GPU, for the ImageNet-1k dataset. On the other hand, Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) needs retraining of the encoder taking about sixty hours on four H100 GPUs.
abstract: Learned representations (or embeddings) are the foundation of modern machine learning systems, yet they are typically trained as fixed-size embeddings, without accounting for varying downstream resource or task constraints. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) addresses this limitation by learning nested representations, but requires costly end-to-end retraining and does not support post hoc expansion, while Contrastive Sparse Representations (CSR) reduce training overhead via lightweight adaptors but operate at a 4x larger dimensionality. Additionally, all prior works restrict their framework towards compression only. In this work, we introduce Hyperbolic Elastic Representation Learning (HERL), a framework for learning dimension-adaptive embeddings (compression and expansion) through a lightweight adaptor without retraining the base encoder. Our key idea is to exploit the exponential capacity of hyperbolic geometry by learning a non-linear mapping from the encoder space to hyperbolic space. We train a simple MLP to downsample the representations before projecting them onto a Lorentzian and learn adaptive representations that respect the Lorentzian geometry. Our approach is model-agnostic and effective in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Through extensive experiments across image and text modalities, we show that HERL preserves downstream performance across a wide range of embedding sizes, exhibits smooth interpolation between dimensions, and achieves these benefits at a fraction of the computational cost.
